quote: stets mindestens eine überzählige Invariante (also n-1 Invari= anten, wenn n der Grad ist und $n > 4$ ist.)?
english: always at least one superfluous invariant (thus n-1 invariants, if n is the degree and n > 4)?
topic: Notes on superfluous invariants of binary forms, on computing the characteristic function for ternary forms (in particular expressing a ternary quartic as $\varphi\psi-\chi^2$, the bitangent problem), and on extending the Cayley-Sylvester counting theorem to ternary forms.

triage.modern_statement: Take the invariant ring R_n = C[S^n C^2]^{SL_2} of binary forms of degree n. For n ≥ 3 its Krull dimension (the number of algebraically independent invariants) is n−2. My reading of Hilbert's question: for n > 4, is there always at least one invariant beyond those n−2 independent ones (an 'überzählige', i.e. superfluous, invariant)? That would mean R_n is never a polynomial ring and needs at least n−1 generators. Equivalently: is R_n free (polynomial) only when n ≤ 4? The bracketed 'n−1 invariants' could also be read as asking whether exactly n−1 invariants are enough. That stronger version is false in general.
triage.answered_by: The lower bound was already clear from 19th-century calculations for small n: Cayley, Clebsch and others found 4 generators with one relation for the quintic, and 5 generators (degrees 2, 4, 6, 10, 15) for the sextic, so already n−1 there. The general statement, that the invariant algebra of an irreducible SL_2-representation is free only in low degree (binary forms of degree ≤ 4), follows from the classification of linear groups with free invariant algebras: Kac–Popov–Vinberg (C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris, 1976) and Adamovich–Golovina / Schwarz (Inventiones, 1978). For larger n the number of generators grows much faster than n−1. For example, degree 10 needs 106 basic invariants, which rules out the 'exactly n−1' reading.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia's survey of small degrees: the invariants of the binary cubic form a polynomial algebra generated by the discriminant. The sextic's invariant algebra is generated in degrees 2, 4, 6, 10, 15, where the first four generate a polynomial ring and the degree-15 invariant is extra. That is a superfluous invariant, giving n−1 = 5 generators.

The binary quintic has four invariants, of degrees 4, 8, 12 and 18. The first three are algebraically independent, and the square of the degree-18 invariant is a polynomial in them. So n=5 needs exactly n−1 = 4 generators, one of them superfluous.

Linear groups with free (polynomial) invariant algebras were classified by Kac, Popov and Vinberg ('Sur les groupes linéaires algébriques dont l'algèbre des invariants est libre') and by Adamovich–Golovina ('Simple linear Lie groups having a free algebra of invariants'). Both are cited in Springer's Invariant Theory of Infinite Groups.
G. Schwarz, 'Representations of simple Lie groups with regular rings of invariants' (Inventiones Math.), another classification of the cases with a polynomial invariant ring.

For binary forms of degree 10 there is a system of parameters of degrees 2, 4, 6, 6, 8, 9, 10, 14 (8 = n−2 elements), and there are 106 basic invariants. So far more than n−1 generators are needed for large n.

triage.why: The note has the vocabulary of Hilbert's 1890–93 work on systems of parameters for invariant rings: n−2 independent invariants, plus the question of whether extra ones are always needed. In modern terms that is the question of whether R_n is a polynomial ring for n > 4. The answer (no, so at least one superfluous invariant is always required) is standard. The sources show it directly for n = 5, 6 and 10, and the 1970s classifications of free invariant algebras settle it in general. One caveat: none of the sources I found states the exact sentence 'free only for n ≤ 4'. For the general case I am relying on the titles of the classification papers, not on their text. The question is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Interpretation risk: if Hilbert meant 'exactly n−1 invariants suffice', the answer is no; that is true only for n = 5 and 6. Either way it is settled. Ongoing work on generators of binary invariants is computation for particular degrees, not this question.
